questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Darwin's theory of how the islands' tortoises evolved into separate species
The long history of buccaneers and whalers who raided the Pacific coast
The political history of the Republic of the Equator and its penal colonies
The Galapagos' volcanic geology, climate, vegetation and settlement as the Beagle found them
questions.explain: The author describes the islands' volcanic craters, climate, vegetation, tortoises and the small colony on Charles Island.

questions.q: What did the author notice about the twenty-eight tuff-craters examined?
options: Their northern sides were lower or broken down
Their southern sides were lower or broken down
Every one contained a small lake of fresh water
They were all active and had erupted recently
questions.explain: Every one of the twenty-eight tuff-craters had a much lower or broken southern side, attributed to waves.

questions.q: On Chatham Island, how many truncated cones did he count from one small eminence?
options: Twenty-eight
Two thousand
Sixty
Seven hundred
questions.explain: From one small eminence he counted sixty black truncated cones, each with a crater.

questions.q: How do the people of Charles Island get their main animal food?
options: From tortoises
From wild pigs
From whaling ships
From goats kept at the coast
questions.explain: The staple article of animal food is supplied by the tortoises, with two days' hunting feeding them for the week.

questions.q: Why are the upper parts of the islands greener than the lower parts?
options: Settlers channel mountain streams to water the upper slopes
Volcanic soil near the summits is far richer in minerals
Low clouds bring moisture, giving the heights a damp climate
Tortoises fertilize the high ground with their droppings
questions.explain: Little rain falls and clouds hang low, so the upper parts, which condense the moisture, are damp and luxuriant while the lower are sterile.
